questions.topic: Conditions — Short-Circuit Evaluation
questions.q: What will this code snippet output?
questions.hint: Recall the evaluation order of the left and right operands of logical AND (&&). Is the right operand evaluated if the left is false?
explanations: Correct! On the first check, the left side `i++ > 0` evaluates `0 > 0` (false), and variable `i` increments to 1. Due to short-circuiting, the right side `++j < 2` is NOT evaluated at all, and `j` remains 0. The loop terminates. Output: "1 0".
Incorrect. Expression `++j` was not executed due to short-circuit evaluation of the `&&` operator.
Incorrect. The loop completed zero iterations, so `i` was incremented only once during the first check.
Incorrect. Postfix increment `i++` executed during condition evaluation, so `i` is not equal to 0.

questions.topic: Comma Operator — Comma in Condition Expression
questions.q: What will the for loop output when using a comma in its condition expression i < 2, j < 5?
questions.hint: The comma operator evaluates the left operand, discards its result, then evaluates and returns the value of the right operand.
explanations: Incorrect. Condition `i < 2` is ignored by the comma operator.
Incorrect. Both variables `i` and `j` are incremented synchronously at each step.

Correct! Expression `i < 2, j < 5` returns exclusively the result of `j < 5`. Condition `i < 2` is evaluated and discarded. The loop continues until `j` equals 5, at which point `i` also becomes 5. Output: "5 5".
Incorrect. Variable `i` does not stop at value 5 until the whole loop stops.
Incorrect. Variable `j` increases and is guaranteed to reach 5.

questions.topic: continue Statement — Behavior Inside do...while
questions.q: Where exactly does the continue statement transfer control in a do...while loop, and what will the code output?
questions.hint: Does continue transfer control to the beginning of the do block or straight to the while condition check at the bottom?
explanations: Correct! In `do...while`, `continue` transfers control directly to condition check `while (i < 3)`. 1) `i=1`: `sum`=1. 2) `i=2`: `continue` jumps to `while(2 < 3)` (true). 3) `i=3`: `sum` = 1 + 3 = 4. `while(3 < 3)` is false. Total: 4.
Incorrect. On the third iteration `i = 3`, condition `i == 2` is false, so 3 is added to `sum`.
Incorrect. Value `i = 2` is skipped due to `continue`, so 2 is not added to `sum`.
Incorrect. Infinite looping does not occur, since `i++` is at the top of the loop body and executes before `continue`.

questions.topic: Control Flow — Interaction of switch and while
questions.q: How do break and continue interact inside a switch statement located inside a while loop?
questions.hint: break exits the switch, while continue moves to the next iteration of the while loop.
explanations: Correct! At `i=0` and `i=1`, `break` executes, exiting `switch` and letting `count++` run (`count` becomes 2). At `i=2`, `continue` executes, which applies to `while` loop and skips `count++`! At `i=3`, `default` triggers, making `count` equal to 3. Answer: 3.
Incorrect. On iteration `i=2`, `continue` call skips `count++` increment.
Incorrect. Iterations `i=0`, `i=1`, and `i=3` are accounted for.
Incorrect. On each iteration `i` increases (`i++`), preventing an infinite loop.

questions.topic: Pointers and Strings — while (*p++) Idiom
questions.q: What will pointer difference p - str equal after executing the compact loop?
questions.hint: Note that pointer increment p++ occurs even when dereferencing symbol *p yields null terminator '\0'.
explanations: Incorrect. 3 is the length of string "Hi!", but the pointer moves one step further past the null terminator.

Correct! String consists of characters 'H' (0), 'i' (1), '!' (2), and '\0' (3). On 4th iteration `*p` reads '\0' (0/false), but postfix `p++` still advances pointer to the next byte (index 4). Difference `(str + 4) - str` equals 4.
Incorrect. The loop stops immediately after reading and advancing past the null terminator.
Incorrect. The very first character 'H' evaluates to true in the condition, so pointer advances further.

questions.topic: Bitwise Operations — Brian Kernighan's Algorithm
questions.q: How many iterations will loop while (n) with operation n &= (n - 1) perform for number n = 13?
questions.hint: Expression n &= (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit (1) in binary representation of the number.
explanations: Incorrect. Number 13 contains more than one set bit in binary form.
Incorrect. Count set bits in binary representation $13_{10} = 1101_2$.
Correct! This is Kernighan's famous algorithm for counting set bits. Binary 13: `1101_2` (three ones). Each iteration clears one set bit: 13 -> 12 -> 8 -> 0. Loop performs exactly 3 iterations.
Incorrect. Binary representation of number 13 has only 3 set bits, not 4.
Incorrect. Loop executes based on set bit count, not numerical value.

questions.topic: Data Types — Signed Overflow
questions.q: What will happen during loop execution with signed 8-bit type signed char c = 125?
questions.hint: Maximum value of signed char is 127. What happens to value c past 127 in two's complement?
explanations: Correct! Iterations: 1) `c=125` (>0), `c` becomes 126, `count`=1. 2) `c=126` (>0), `c` becomes 127, `count`=2. 3) `c=127` (>0), `c` overflows to -128, `count`=3. 4) `c=-128` (not >0), loop breaks. Total `count` = 3.
Incorrect. Loop started at value 125, not 1.
Incorrect. Counter counts actually completed iterations.
Incorrect. Overflowing to negative value -128 leads to check `-128 > 0` (false) and stops.

questions.topic: C Idioms — Using do...while(0) in Macros
questions.q: Why are multi-line C macros almost always wrapped in a do { ... } while(0) construct?
questions.hint: Think about what happens if a multi-statement macro is expanded inside an if (cond) MACRO(); else ... branch without curly braces.
options: To combine multiple statements into a single syntactic block safe for expansion in if-else branches
To force the macro to run in a separate isolated thread
To optimize code execution speed at processor level
explanations: Correct! The `do { ... } while(0)` construct groups statements and requires a trailing semicolon after `MACRO();`. This prevents 'dangling else' syntax errors when expanding the macro inside `if (cond) MACRO(); else ...`.
Incorrect. Macros are simple preprocessor text substitutions; they do not create threads.
Incorrect. The compiler optimizes `while(0)`, completely removing the loop structure from final machine code.
Incorrect. C macro expansions do not support recursion.

questions.topic: Nested Loops — Dependent Loop Limits
questions.q: What does the sum calculated in nested loops with dependent limit j <= i equal?
questions.hint: Write out iterations: at i=1 adds 1; at i=2 adds (1+2); at i=3 adds (1+2+3).
explanations: Incorrect. 6 is the sum of only the final outer iteration (1+2+3).
Incorrect. Check addition accuracy at each step.
Correct! i=1: sum += 1 (sum=1). i=2: sum += 1 + 2 (sum=4). i=3: sum += 1 + 2 + 3 (sum=10). Final value of `sum` equals 10.
Incorrect. Range of `i` is bounded by value 3.
Incorrect. That would be result for `i` from 1 to 5.

questions.topic: Lifetime and Scope — Static Inside Loop Body
questions.q: How does variable static int k = 5 declared inside a for loop body behave?
questions.hint: Static variables (static) are initialized only ONCE prior to program execution, not on each iteration.
explanations: Incorrect. Static variable retains its value between iterations, rather than resetting to 5.
Incorrect. Check accumulated value of `k` at steps `i=0, 1, 2`.
Correct! `k` is initialized to 5 once. Iteration 0: `k`=5+0=5, `res`=5. Iteration 1: `k`=5+1=6, `res`=5+6=11. Iteration 2: `k`=6+2=8, `res`=11+8=19. Output: 19.
Incorrect. Variable `i` takes values 0, 1, and 2 (3 iterations total).

questions.topic: Unsigned Types — Risks of i >= 0 Check for unsigned
questions.q: Why would condition unsigned int i; i >= 0 without early break lead to an infinite loop?
questions.hint: Can an unsigned integer (unsigned) take a negative value?
explanations: Incorrect. Counter will manage to exceed 5.
Incorrect. At `count = 5`, condition `count > 5` is still false; exit happens on next step.

Correct! Unsigned number `unsigned` is always `>= 0`. At `i = 0`, step `i--` turns `i` into `UINT_MAX`. Without protection `if (count > 5) break;`, loop would be infinite. With protection, `count` increments 6 times until `break` triggers. Output: 6.
Incorrect. Safety `break` is present in code, preventing infinite looping.

questions.topic: Loop Control — Semantics of continue in Nesting
questions.q: Which statement regarding continue in nested loops is true?
questions.hint: Does continue affect outer loops?
options: continue transfers control to header/condition of ONLY the innermost loop inside which it is invoked
continue terminates execution of current function and returns 0
continue resets and restarts the outermost loop
explanations: Correct! The `continue` statement interrupts only the current iteration of the innermost loop and transfers control to its step/condition section.
Incorrect. To terminate a function, the `return` statement is used.
Incorrect. `continue` does not directly affect outer loops.

questions.topic: C Optimization and Tricks — Duff's Device
questions.q: What is the classic construct 'Duff's Device' famous for in C programming?
questions.hint: Think about loop unrolling and overlapping control structures.
options: Unusual interleaving of switch statement and do...while loop for effective loop unrolling
A technique for buffer overflow protection in strcpy and strcat functions
A method for quicksorting arrays without using recursion
An algorithm for detecting memory leaks on heap
explanations: Correct! Tom Duff devised interleaving `switch` and `do...while`, where `case` labels lie inside the loop body. This allows efficient block copying with partial loop unrolling.
Incorrect. This is a loop optimization pattern, not a string validator.
Incorrect. Duff's device has no relation to sorting algorithms.
Incorrect. It does not track `malloc` memory allocations.

questions.topic: String Copying — Classic while ((*d++ = *s++)) Loop
questions.q: What will be stored in array dest after executing loop while ((*d++ = *s++));?
questions.hint: Assignment operation = returns assigned value. When '\0' is assigned, expression returns 0 (false).
explanations: Correct! This is a canonical C string copying idiom. Characters 'A', 'B', and '\0' are sequentially copied from `src` to `dest`. When `'\0'` is copied, expression returns 0 and loop terminates. `dest` will hold complete string "AB".
Incorrect. Loop will not stop at first character; it copies entire string including null terminator.
Incorrect. First characters 'A' and 'B' have non-zero ASCII codes, so condition evaluates successfully.

questions.topic: Control Flow — Jumping into Loop via goto
questions.q: What will the program output if making an unconditional goto jump directly inside a while loop body?
questions.hint: Trace flow: goto jumps to label target:, executes x *= 2, reaches end of loop body, and moves to standard check x < 3.
explanations: Incorrect. After first operation `x` becomes 2, but loop performs another full pass.
Incorrect. Count addition and multiplication operations on second pass.

Correct! 1) `goto target`: jump inside, `x *= 2` (`x`=2). 2) Check condition `while (2 < 3)` -> true! 3) Loop entry from top: `x++` (`x`=3), then `target:` `x *= 2` (`x`=6). 4) Check `while (6 < 3)` -> false! Loop exit. Answer: 6.
Incorrect. Second iteration increases `x` from 2 to 3 prior to multiplication.
Incorrect. `goto` jump to label inside loop is completely legal in C (unless skipping VLA initialization).

questions.topic: C Standards — Unsequenced Modifications
questions.q: What effect does expression arr[i] = i++ inside a loop lead to in modern C standards (C99/C11/C17)?
questions.hint: Think about whether evaluation order of array index on the left and side effect i++ on the right is guaranteed.
explanations: Incorrect. Code has no guaranteed result.
Incorrect. C standards contain no rule requiring left side of assignment to be evaluated first.
Correct! In expression `arr[i] = i++`, reading and modification of variable `i` occur without a sequence point between them. This is classic Undefined Behavior (UB).
Incorrect. Compiler will compile this code, possibly issuing a warning.

questions.topic: Data Types — Overflow of unsigned char in Condition Comparison
questions.q: What will happen when attempting to execute for (i = 250; i < 256; i++) loop with 8-bit unsigned char variable?
questions.hint: Recall value range of 8-bit unsigned char type (0 to 255). Can it ever reach 256?
explanations: Incorrect. 8-bit `unsigned char` cannot physically hold value 256.
Incorrect. Due to infinite looping, code will not reach execution of `printf`.
Incorrect. Loop will not terminate at value 255.
Correct! Maximum value of 8-bit `unsigned char` is 255. When `i` equals 255, `i++` operation overflows and resets `i` to 0. Since `0 < 256` is always true, loop becomes infinite.

questions.topic: Preprocessor — Macro Expansion Errors in Loop Headers
questions.q: What will variable sum equal due to specifics of macro substitution MULTIPLY(1 + 1, 2)?
questions.hint: Substitute arguments into macro literally: 1 + 1 * 2 without adding outer parentheses.
explanations: Incorrect. Loop will complete more than one iteration.
Incorrect. Due to operator precedence, condition result will be greater than 2.

Correct! Preprocessor performs simple text substitution. Expression `MULTIPLY(1 + 1, 2)` expands to `1 + 1 * 2`. Arithmetic rules dictate multiplication first: $1 + (1 \times 2) = 3$. Condition becomes `i < 3`. Loop executes 3 iterations, and `sum` becomes 3.
Incorrect. Expected mathematical result `(1+1)*2 = 4` failed due to missing parentheses in macro definition.

questions.topic: Scope — Shadowing of Loop Variables
questions.q: What will printf output after loop execution where variable int x with same name is declared inside?
questions.hint: Variable x declared in for (int x = ...) header shadows outer x only within its own block.
explanations: Incorrect. Inner variable `x`, reaching 3, is destroyed upon exiting loop.
Correct! Declaring `int x` inside `for` header creates a new local variable shadowing outer `x = 10`. All modifications affect inner variable. Outer variable `x` remains intact and equals 10.
Incorrect. Outer `x` was not reset to 0.
Incorrect. Declaring variable with same name in nested scope block is syntactically allowed in C.

questions.topic: Pointers and Arrays — Layout of Multidimensional Arrays in Memory
questions.q: Is traversing 2D array int a[2][2] using a single pointer int *p valid?
questions.hint: In C, elements of multidimensional arrays are guaranteed to lie contiguously in memory (row-major order).
explanations: Correct! Elements of a multidimensional array in C lie continuously in memory: `a[0][0]`, `a[0][1]`, `a[1][0]`, `a[1][1]`. Pointer `p` sequentially visits all elements: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.
Incorrect. Because memory is guaranteed contiguous, this traversal is fully standard.
Incorrect. Expression `&a[0][0]` has type `int*`, compatible with `int *p`.
Incorrect. Loop sums values of elements (1+2+3+4), not their count.

questions.topic: volatile Keyword — Preventing Optimization of Busy-Wait Loops
questions.q: For what purpose is a flag variable in busy-wait loops like while (!flag) declared with the volatile qualifier?
questions.hint: Think about what the compiler optimizer will do if variable flag is not modified by explicit instructions INSIDE the loop body.
options: To prevent compiler optimization that might cache the variable value in a CPU register, creating an infinite loop
To make reading and writing this variable atomic at hardware level
To forbid other functions from changing this variable's value
To speed up loop execution by placing variable in L1 cache
explanations: Correct! Without `volatile`, the compiler sees that `flag` does not change inside the `while` body, and may read it into a register only ONCE before the loop. The `volatile` qualifier forces the compiler to re-read the value from memory on EVERY iteration.
Incorrect. `volatile` in C does not provide atomicity or inter-thread synchronization.
Incorrect. Protection against modification uses `const`, not `volatile`.
Incorrect. `volatile` may actually decrease speed because it disables register caching.

questions.topic: for Header — Execution Order of Expressions in Step Section
questions.q: What will the program output after executing empty-body loop for (; i < 5; i++, sum += i) ;?
questions.hint: Trace order of execution for comma-separated step i++ and summation sum += i.
explanations: Incorrect. Note that `i++` occurs BEFORE evaluating `sum += i` in step section.

Correct! On each step, `i++` is evaluated first (incrementing `i`), and then across sequence point (comma), `sum += i` is evaluated using UPDATED `i`. Iteration 1: i=1, sum=1. Iteration 2: i=2, sum=1+2=3. Iteration 3: i=3, sum=3+3=6. Iteration 4: i=4, sum=6+4=10. Iteration 5: i=5, sum=10+5=15. Condition `5 < 5` breaks loop. Result: "5 15".
Incorrect. Loop terminates only when `i` equals 5.
Incorrect. Variable `sum` accumulates values of all intermediate `i`.

questions.topic: Control Flow — Switch Fallthrough Inside Loops
questions.q: What will variable sum equal after executing a for loop with a switch that partially lacks break statements?
questions.hint: Trace case 0 carefully: absence of break falls through directly into case 1.
explanations: Incorrect. You overlooked fallthrough from `case 0` into `case 1`.

Correct! 1) `i=0`: `case 0` executes (`sum`+=1), falls through to `case 1` (`sum`+=2), and hits `break` (`sum` = 3). 2) `i=1`: `case 1` executes (`sum`+=2) and hits `break` (`sum` = 5). 3) `i=2`: `case 2` executes (`sum`+=3) (`sum` = 8). Output: 8.
Incorrect. Check addition for each iteration `i = 0, 1, 2`.
Incorrect. Third iteration at `i=2` adds 3 to current sum.

questions.topic: C Standards — Signed and Unsigned Type Overflow
questions.q: What is the fundamental difference in C standards regarding overflow of signed versus unsigned types in loops?
questions.hint: Recall which type's behavior is strictly specified by modulo $2^N$ math, and which is UB.
options: Unsigned type overflow is strictly defined (modulo $2^N$ arithmetic), while signed overflow causes Undefined Behavior (UB)
Signed type overflow is strictly defined, while unsigned overflow causes Undefined Behavior (UB)
Overflow of both types leads to Undefined Behavior (UB)
Both types safely wrap around modulo $2^N$
explanations: Correct! Under ISO C standard, unsigned type overflow is strictly defined as modulo $2^N$ arithmetic. Meanwhile, signed type overflow is Undefined Behavior (UB), allowing the compiler to optimize or eliminate loops.
Incorrect. The exact opposite is true: `unsigned` is protected by standard, whereas `signed` causes UB.
Incorrect. Unsigned types in C never trigger UB on arithmetic overflow.
Incorrect. Signed types have no standard guarantee of wrapping around modulo $2^N$.

questions.topic: Data Structures — Classic Singly Linked List Traversal Loop

Incorrect. Pointer `curr` is initially initialized with address `&a`, so loop executes.
Incorrect. Last structure `c` contains `NULL` in `next` field, breaking condition `curr != NULL`.

questions.topic: Logic Errors — Assignment = Instead of Comparison == in while
questions.q: What will printf output after executing code with loop while (x = 0)?

explanations: Correct! Expression `x = 0` assigns value 0 to variable `x` and returns this assigned value (0/false). Loop body executes ZERO times. Variable `x` remains 0. Prints 0.
Incorrect. Due to assignment operator `x = 0`, value of variable `x` changed before condition check.
Incorrect. Loop body `x++` was not executed due to false condition.
Incorrect. Expression `x = 0` evaluates to 0 (false), terminating loop immediately.

questions.topic: break Statement — Counter State Upon Early Exit
questions.q: What value will counter i retain immediately after break triggers under condition i == 2?
questions.hint: Does step section i++ execute when the break statement runs?
explanations: Correct! On iteration `i = 2`, condition `i == 2` evaluates to true and `break` is called. The `break` statement instantly exits loop, skipping increment section `i++`. Value of `i` remains 2.
Incorrect. Step `i++` is evaluated only AFTER loop body completion, which code does not reach due to `break`.
Incorrect. At `i = 1`, condition `1 == 2` was false, progressing to next iteration.
Incorrect. Counter managed to increase to 2.

questions.topic: Complex Loops — Ternary Operator in Step Section
questions.q: How many iterations will a for loop complete when its step depends on the parity of variable i?
questions.hint: Trace changes in i: 0 (even -> +1) -> 1 (odd -> +2) -> 3 (odd -> +2) -> 5.
explanations: Correct! 1st iteration: `i=0`, `count=1`. Step: 0 is even, `i += 1` (becomes 1). 2nd iteration: `i=1`, `count=2`. Step: 1 is odd, `i += 2` (becomes 3). 3rd iteration: `i=3`, `count=3`. Step: 3 is odd, `i += 2` (becomes 5). Check `5 < 5` stops loop. Total: 3 iterations.
Incorrect. Trace step at `i = 1`, 2 is added, not 1.
Incorrect. Loop skips even values `i = 2` and `i = 4`.
Incorrect. Loop will complete 3 full steps.

questions.topic: Pointers and Arrays — One-Past-The-End Pointer
questions.q: Is expression int *end = arr + 3 legal in C and what is the loop result?
questions.hint: The C standard allows computing address of element immediately AFTER last array element, provided it is NOT dereferenced.
options: Yes, it is a fully legal 'past-the-end' pointer, sum equals 60
No, creating pointer arr + 3 causes Undefined Behavior
explanations: Correct! The C standard guarantees that obtaining a pointer to element immediately past array end (one-past-the-end) is legal and can be used for comparisons (`p < end`). Dereferencing it is prohibited, but loop dereferences only `p < end`. Result: 10 + 20 + 30 = 60.
Incorrect. UB occurs only on attempted DEREFERENCING (`*end`), not when computing or comparing address.
Incorrect. Pointer arithmetic with arrays is fully supported by compiler.
Incorrect. Loop sums all three array elements.
